subject: Anatomy
summary: The sacrum is a triangular bone formed by five fused vertebrae, linking the spine to the pelvis. It transmits weight to the hips and houses sacral nerves that control lower limb and pelvic functions.

sections.p: The sacrum sits at the base of the spine, forming the posterior wall of the pelvis and articulating with the ilia at the sacroiliac joints.
b: Divides the pelvic cavity into true and false pelvis

sections.p: It lies between L5 and the coccyx, with a broad superior surface and a narrow inferior apex.
b: Anterior surface: sacral canal, sacral foramina
Posterior surface: sacral ala, median sacral crest

sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the rectum, uterus, and bladder; laterally the sacroiliac joints bind it to the pelvis; posteriorly the gluteal muscles attach.
b: Piriformis and gluteus maximus insert on the sacral ala
Levator ani and coccygeus arise from the posterior surface

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the sacrum via the median sacral artery and branches of the internal iliac system.
The sacral spinal nerves (S1‑S5) exit through the sacral foramina, forming the sacral plexus that innervates the lower limb and pelvic organs.
b: Anterior sacral foramina → ventral rami (sacral plexus)

sections.p: It provides a sturdy platform for weight transfer from the spine to the hips and protects the sacral nerve roots.
b: Transmits axial load during walking and lifting

sections.p: Fractures, sacroiliac joint dysfunction, and sacral nerve compression can cause pain, gait disturbance, and bowel/bladder dysfunction.
b: Traumatic fracture: often from falls or motor‑vehicle accidents
Sacroiliac joint sprain: common in pregnancy, heavy lifting
Cauda equina syndrome: compression of sacral roots, surgical emergency

t.b: Detects sacral fractures or dislocation; if unavailable, use clinical instability signs
Assesses nerve root compression or cauda equina; if unavailable, urgent CT can rule out bony injury
Defines complex fracture patterns; if unavailable, treat based on exam and plain radiograph

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Palpate sacral hiatus for caudal epidural access
Assess sacroiliac tenderness with FABER test
Check for perineal sensation loss in sacral nerve injury

whenToSeekHelp: Severe lower back pain with saddle anesthesia
Loss of bladder or bowel control after trauma
Progressive weakness of legs with numbness

faq.q: Why does a sacral fracture cause urinary problems?
faq.a: The sacral nerves (S2‑S4) control bladder function; fracture can compress them, leading to retention or incontinence.

faq.q: What is the difference between sacral and coccygeal pain?
faq.a: Sacral pain is higher, often linked to weight‑bearing or nerve injury; coccygeal pain is localized to the tailbone and worsens with sitting.

faq.q: How can I differentiate sacroiliac joint sprain from lumbar strain?
faq.a: Sacroiliac pain radiates to the groin or posterior thigh and is provoked by FABER or Gaenslen tests; lumbar strain worsens with flexion/extension.

exam: Describe the articulations of the sacrum and their clinical significance.
Explain how a sacral fracture can lead to cauda equina syndrome and what signs you would look for.
Identify the nerves that exit the sacral foramina and the muscles they supply.
